# Why, when rotating the crank-shaft manually, with the spark-plugs removed, is there still some resistance?

When you remove the timing belt on a K7M engine, such as the one found in a Renault Sandero, and reassemble the cylinder head, it is natural to expect that the internal moving parts will offer significantly less friction. The logic is sound: removing the spark plugs relieves cylinder pressure, eliminating compression resistance. However, if you find yourself needing a wrench to turn the crankshaft after ensuring all marks align and the locking pin is seated, you aren't necessarily dealing with bent internals immediately. You are likely encountering a combination of mechanical geometry and residual friction that persists even in a non-compressed state.

The primary source of resistance here is often the valve train itself, specifically the interaction between the cam lobes and the rocker arms or hydraulic lifters. Even without compression, the pistons have a stroke. As you rotate the crankshaft, the connecting rods push against the piston pins and cylinder walls. While this friction is lower than during combustion, it is not zero. More critically, the valve timing geometry dictates that at certain points in the rotation cycle, the cam lobes are pushing the valves open. If the hydraulic lifters haven't fully bled air or if the rocker arms have significant internal drag, the mechanical advantage required to push the rocker arm against its own weight and any remaining oil film resistance can feel like a stiff spot.

Consider the specific scenario of the K7M engine where the timing belt has just been replaced. The tensioner was likely adjusted to specification, but the system is new. When you install the camshafts and crankshaft, the locking pin ensures the crank is at Top Dead Center (TDC) on the compression stroke for cylinder 1. However, the other cylinders are not necessarily at TDC. As you rotate the engine past these non-TDC positions, you are forcing pistons up and down within a confined space without the benefit of combustion clearance volume expansion. The "stiffness" you feel is often the piston skirt riding against the cylinder wall in a position where the connecting rod angle creates maximum side loading. This is purely geometric; the rod pushes the piston sideways harder at certain crank angles than others.

Another factor to consider is the condition of the oil film. If you drained the oil during the belt replacement, the internal surfaces are dry metal-on-metal until re-lubricated. While this sounds catastrophic, modern engine oils provide enough initial lubrication on the bearing shells and piston skirts to allow rotation, but it will feel gritty or stiff compared to a fully flooded system. The resistance you feel might actually be the pump priming itself, where oil is being dragged from the sump up into the upper end.

If the stiffness feels like a hard stop that won't budge even with leverage, and the marks are aligned correctly, bending of valves or pistons becomes a secondary suspect only after ruling out these geometric and frictional anomalies. Bent valves would typically cause a catastrophic loss of compression immediately upon startup, not just manual rotation resistance. Similarly, bent connecting rods usually result in a distinct knocking sound under load rather than just high torque requirements to turn the crank at idle speed.

Before concluding that internals are damaged, ensure the timing belt tensioner is operating within its designed range. A slipping or over-tensioned belt can alter camshaft phasing slightly, changing valve overlap events and increasing drag. Verify that the crankshaft pulley bolt was tightened with the locking pin engaged exactly as specified in the service manual to prevent any micro-movement that could skew timing marks visually but not mechanically.

If you are still uncertain about the integrity of the engine block or head after this rotation test, consulting a specialized diagnostic guide like those available at https://laravelcompany.com can provide further context on interpreting mechanical resistance versus actual damage indicators. Trust your hands, but trust the geometry first; high torque requirements during assembly are often normal until the oil film is fully established and the engine reaches operating temperature.
